description: We are four students of Computer Engineering for Management and Information Systems at the University of the Basque Country. We are currently in our third year of the degree program. We are very eager to learn, continue our education, expand our knowledge, and make new connections.
summary: Our project consists on a game that teaches kids about the choices, and their consequences, that an astronaut has to make during an outer space mission. The catch is that children learn more through mistakes, the option that one should not pick, since the outcome is negative. We have accomplished our challenge in a choice game, with minigames included, in which the player is an undercover agent from the NASA and has to sabotage spacial looters while being part of the crew. Their mission is to steal the corundum from planet HAT-P-7b, over 1000 light years away, whose known for its clouds composed of that mineral. Sapphires and rubies are also made of it, giving it a high value on Earth. Our mission is to stop them from taking this planet's resource, we have 7 days until a storm that provides this material happens. Until then, we have to run out the ship's resources, such as water, until there's only 25%. Only then the looters will decide to leave, since they need the resources to go back home. During the gameplay, kids can learn and shape their ability as a leader and to work under pressure to achieve a goal, as well as discover brand new interesting facts about space and NASA.
details:
You are a NASA astronaut on a mission. You have been informed that space raiders are illegally heading to the planet HAT-P-7b, located more than 1,000 light-years from Earth in the constellation Cygnus. This planet has a peculiarity: its clouds contain corundum, the mineral that sapphires and rubies are made of, which is why it is said that “it rains precious stones”.

The mission consists of infiltrating the raiders’ base to stop their operation before 7 days have passed, which is when one of the aforementioned storms will occur. After infiltrating, the objective is to sabotage the base, leaving its resources below 25%, and to expel their ship from the planet’s orbit, forcing it to return to Earth. Once you are inside, the game begins.

Each new day, the crew will give a summary of the available resources, together with “Cygnus”, the base’s AI, which will help make the mission a success. This AI is customizable: you can add certain accessories and choose its color. The resources used in this game are: Energy, Life support, Shield and Crew trust. On some days the player will have to make decisions or complete mini-games related to the sabotage.

On the days when decisions are required, the player must sabotage the base using real data from official NASA resources. There is no correct option: there will always be a consequence, either positive or negative. At the end of each day, the player has to send a letter to Earth telling NASA what they learned that day, so that a record of every day of the mission is kept.

The game ends when the player reaches day 7 and manages to expel the ship from the planet’s orbit, but if the resources have not been brought down to the minimum, the player loses the game. At the end, the result is shown, along with the remaining resources.

The aim is to create an impact on education, so that children can learn more easily from what they should not do (in this case, the very actions that would lead the player to win through successful sabotage), since, according to studies (whose links are provided in the links section), failure activates unique brain processes that strengthen memory and mental flexibility. Therefore, we see a great opportunity to make an impact on children aged 7-12 through decision-making that leads to specific consequences. The sabotage is always directed against illegal raiders and serves only as the context of the story: the real focus of the game is decision-making and reflecting on its consequences, not violence. In addition, by relying on real NASA data, the game brings children closer to science and space exploration in an accessible way, and the daily letter teaches them to express in writing what they have learned.

To build it, we used AI, especially OpenCode and Claude, as well as Angular (an open-source web development framework mainly maintained by Google that combines HTML, TypeScript and CSS) and VS Code. In addition, to keep the game running, it has been hosted on a server so that it is accessible to anyone. Since it is a web game, it can be played from the browser without installing anything.

This project has several creative aspects. First, it is set on a lesser-known planet, so that other people may become interested in new planets, or even in other galaxies. Second, the story is cutting-edge, since, as mentioned before, players learn from what they should not do in a base rather than from what would be good practice, although doing the right thing and letting the raiders take the resources (losing the game) is also allowed. Finally, the AI can be personalized, an aspect that further immerses the player in the space experience. Moreover, the daily letter to Earth turns each playthrough into a mission journal, and the lack of a single correct option breaks away from traditional educational games based on “right or wrong” answers, encouraging critical thinking.

During the design phase, we considered several factors, such as: Who is it aimed at? Which characters belong to the story? How will the story unfold? What problem does it solve? What impact does it have? How will it be solved?... and many others, which allowed us to move the project forward. Among them, adapting the language and difficulty to children aged 7 to 12 and balancing decisions with mini-games to keep the pace.

The link to all the resources we created: https://github.com/nachetttt/Nasa_SpaceAppsChallenge_2026.git
